newsitem.title: USA: "The Fugitive" case gets DNA tests.
newsitem.headline: "The Fugitive" case gets DNA tests.

text.p: A DNA expert said on Tuesday that a third person may have been present at the bludgeoning death more than 40 years ago of the wife of an Ohio osteopath who was the inspiration for "The Fugitive" TV series and movie.

Dr. Sam Sheppard was convicted of second-degree murder in the 1954 killing of his wife Marilyn but was acquitted in a new trial in 1966. Until his death in 1970 he maintained that a bushy-haired intruder had knocked him unconscious the night of the murder but such an intruder was never found.

Dr. Mohammad Tahir, an Indianapolis DNA expert hired by Sheppard's son, said at a news conference that DNA tests he conducted on blood samples saved from the case indicated a third person was present, corroborating Sheppard.

"The evidence proves that Dr. Sheppard is not the killer," Terry Gilbert, a Cleveland lawyer working with Tahir, said. "There is no forensic evidence linking Dr. Sheppard to this case and there never has been."
Marilyn Sheppard, 31 and pregnant, was beaten to death at the couple's suburban Bay Village home July 4, 1954. Within six months, Sheppard was sentenced to life in prison.

Unlike the fictional "fugitive", Dr. Richard Kimble, who claimed a one-armed man was the real killer, Sheppard did not escape. He spent 10 years behind bars before a judge freed him in 1964, ruling excessive media coverage tainted the original trial. A second jury acquitted him. He died in 1970 at age 46.

The couple's son, Sam Reese Sheppard, was a 7-year-old boy asleep at home at the time of the murder. He filed a civil lawsuit in 1995 against Ohio asking the state to declare his father innocent and pay compensation of at least $250,000 for the decade his father spent in prison.

The son's legal team said their tests proved a third person was present because blood splattered at the scene was not Mrs. Sheppard's and it was shown at the time of the killing that Dr. Sheppard had no wounds that bled.

They suggested as a "solid suspect" Richard Eberling, 67, who washed windows for the Sheppards and who is serving a life sentence for killing another woman. Eberling provided a blood sample for tests but has denied killing Marilyn Sheppard.
Gilbert said DNA tests did not prove Eberling was at the murder scene but indicated he cannot be ruled out as a suspect.

First Assistant Cuyahoga County Prosecutor Carmen Marino, representing the state in the civil suit, said he is not certain the new evidence establishes the presence of a third person, but "there are some real issues raised," he said.
